title: Just Cause
text: (Full disclosure: I rushed through this game's story while doing barely any sidequests or collectible missions, just so I could write this review before I finished Just Cause 3 and wrote its review. Don't worry, I'm going to come back and do some more optional stuff at some point.) It's interesting to see the progression of the Just Cause series, to watch it come ever closer to what I call the "Just Cause Idea". The Just Cause Idea, for the record, is as follows: In a massive, beautiful, island nation (around 1000 square kilometers) run by a cartoonishly evil dictator, Rico Rodriguez, the world's most physics-defying Hispanic man, must use his huge amounts of mobility and destruction potential to bring down the dictator's rule by breaking everything the dictator owns. And it only gets more fun the more you play it. The original Just Cause is a fairly generic game, obviously heavily inspired by old-school shooters as well as Grand Theft Autos 3, Vice City, and San Andreas. You run around shooting and driving cars and breaking things and holding an anomalous amount of guns, constantly maintaining a baseline level of fun; enough to keep you occupied but not exactly enthrall you. However, the first stirrings of the Just Cause Idea are also apparent. You have infinite parachutes; a primitive, vehicles-only version of the later games' hookshot; no regard for civilian lives; a massive island nation run by a cartoonishly evil dictator; and more time spent in freefall than a professional skydiver. And, of course, you're (young) Rico Rodriguez. In Just Cause 2, the Just Cause Idea is advanced even further, and the game is far better for it. Your grappling hook is no longer a weapon but a permanant staple that changes the game forever, Rico's defiance of physics gets f*cking insane, the shooting becomes merely a placeholder to simply add challenge to all the movement and destruction, the world becomes more diverse, the graphics get prettier (to the point that the atmospheric effects will probably never be outdone), there's more and cooler stuff to destroy in cooler ways, the villain gets even more cartoonish, and the game is overall more engaging, fun, and just...wonderful. The Just Cause Idea proves its worth in this game. Just Cause 3 is probably the most perfect and complete realization of an idea ever, but I'm saving that for the review. If I were to use a metaphor to describe the series' progression, it'd probably go as thus: Just Cause 1 is a flower starting to bud, the colorful petals just beginning to show from in between the sepals; Just Cause 2 is that flower in full bloom, its colors open for all to see; and Just Cause 3 is the flower if it were to detach entirely from the plant it budded from, becoming a spherical mass of petals and floating off to live in its own little world of explosions and madness. Anyway, Just Cause is still a fine game in its own right. Great? Not quite; it's the weakest of the series in my opinion, with its technological limitations and conventionality preventing it from reaching the same dizzying heights as its successors. But it's pretty good, and I guess it's worth buying, especially if you're as invested in the series as I am or if it's on sale.

title: Just Cause
text: Pros: As GTA3 clones go, adding extreme sports and OTT stunts is one of the ideas that make it worthwhile, introducing things that you find yourself wishing were in GTA3. Tremendous freedom, with multiple approaches to two thirds of the main missions(parachute in, burst through the front, sneak in, etc.). If you're in a vehicle moving fast, or you make a vertical jump of about a dozen meters or more, you can engage your parachute, from where you can comfortably shoot or grapple to any vehicle. Shooting is like a proper third person shooter, not like GTA3 and Vice City. Vehicles include cars, motorcycles, boats, helicopters and planes, all of these types can come armed with machineguns and/or rockets, and all of them useful: sail, since you're in an island paradise, and going across water may be the shortest distance between two points; helicopter flight is easily the most flexible way to travel, because of mountains and sea; and planes are by far the fastest way to travel far. Control is great, no matter what you travel by. Fairly challenging. Limits on ammo and weapon carry capacity(two pistols, two types of C4, and another two guns - choose carefully between SMGs, assault and sniper rifles, RPGs and a grenade launcher) ensure that you are careful in shootouts. A fun arcade game. Cons: Very clearly rushed, with glitches and bugs. Nothing to do once you've completed the short story and liberated all enemy zones and/or completed a certain number of the uninspired, crushingly inconsequential and repetitive side-missions. Characters are bland, and there's little to the story, meaning there's almost no "meat" to what's going on(the fun stuff is all in the game-play). Over half of the large island nation is forest and sea. Too many story missions are samey. My recommendation: If you can live with its rather rough edges, this is among the most fun open-world games.

title: Kentucky Route Zero
text: Kentucky Route Zero is best described as an interactive visual novel, along the lines of Superbrothers: Sword & Sorcery EP. There is a huge amount of talent being demonstrated here, and primarily for that reason I'm ultimately going to give this game the thumbs up. Unlike related games such as the marginally more successful The Walking Dead, however, it left me with little real feeling of player agency. Sure, there is some flexibility to move around and experience different absurdist vignettes between story-arc set pieces, however for the most part these don't pretend to influence the narrative progression in any observable way. The game doesn't demonstrate any noticeable sense of self-awareness about this either, like in The Stanley Parable. Ultimately, the best comparison I can draw is to meditative extended video-clips, such as Baraka and Powaqqatsi, in that this game is a thing that exists primarily to be watched and admired. As a meditation to be watched and admired, this game succeeds admirably. The block colour/silhouette style is gorgeous; the audio sparse and evocative; and the melancholy dialogue intelligent, mature and well written. The setting is whimsical and dream-like, with absurdist elements, and the pacing and tone works well in the context. I'm on the fence, however, about whether I think that Kentucky Route Zero is any good as a game. As I would define a 'game', player agency seems to me a defining characteristic. Agency might be via micro-decisions, such as what to shoot in a linear FPS, stat progression trees and character customisation in an RPG, or varying strategic and tactical choices influenced by the randomness of procedural generation. It is the perception of player agency, even if only a perception, that adds a level of immersion that allows one to be drawn into a story and personally invest in it. In Kentucky Route Zero, while the player moves various protagonists around the screen and clicks dialogue choices, these rarely have any noticeable influence on the story other than exposition. I therefore find myself drawing comparisons with other, more established, non-interactive media, such as graphic novels, literature and film that are more reliant on narrative and where examples of mature, quality story lines are plentiful. How, then, does this game compare to great film, great literature, or a great graphic novel? On that basis Kentucky Route Zero can reasonably claim to be good, I think, but not quite great. Ultimately, if I want to be taken for a ride I actually get better immersion from letting a story wash over me while reading or watching a movie. At Kentucky Route Zero's pace, the interaction can tend to break immersion rather than enhances it. It does seem to me, however, that there may be a tendency for those well aware of the woeful absence of genuinely intelligent, complex and mature themes in most games to be a tad overenthusiastic when they find a game that does take a decent stab at these, even if it fails on virtually every other measure by which we normally assess computer games (Rock Paper Shotgun 2013 GOTY, I'm looking at you). Having said that, after now playing through Episode III, I feel compelled to add that for the first third of this installment the game genuinely transcends its limitations to become something truly sublime. It is therefore even more of a disappointment when the remaining two thirds of the same episode drops the ball a little on several levels. Nonetheless, there is certainly potential for masterpiece if the game's best form can be recaptured for the remaining episodes. Having now played through Episode III after decent break from the release of Episode II, it is also worth adding that the game doesn't hold up at all well to extended pauses between episodes. The complexity and nuance of the characters and story, one of the game's big selling points, is also its biggest downfall as the minutiae is particularly hard to recall several months down the track. For this reason, I'd urge people to consider resisting the need for instant gratification and wait for the complete five episode experience. Episode III is slightly longer than the first two episodes, possibly due to some repetitiveness. With two more episodes to go, one might estimate that a full meandering playthrough will likely take around 9 hours, which seems fair for a game of this type. .

title: Kentucky Route Zero
text: A triumph of the p&c medium. I never knew I wanted a point and click magical realist game, but here it is, and I never want to stop playing it. It's perfect in it's execution of it too. It's dark and mysterious enough that it could have been a straight up horror game, but it never really gets thematically dark enough to be truly horror. It's just..so wonderfully realized and consistent in it's symbolism. Lots of these artsy games try so hard to be deep that they come off as snobby at best and embarassingly up-their-own-a$$ at worst. This never does that, telling exactly the story it means to tell without being to minimal, or too florid. I'll stop gushing about this game after I say how amazing, tight, ingenious and sublime the camera is. As the camera follows you around it reveals things you wouldn't otherwise have seen if you had just pointed and clicked at the items on the screen. It's an incentive to go exploring because you're rewarded with these vast beautiful cinematic vistas with weird and wonderful sights to behold that were waiting for you just offscreen. I'd recommend this game to anyone that likes surrealism. I also liked the bears. Plz #5 soon.

title: Kentucky Route Zero
text: Sometimes when you're flying through space you end up meeting a robot. Sometimes that robot is wearing a dress and rides a motorcycle with another robot. Sometimes that robot plays the keytar and likes to sing in dive bars. Sometimes that robot knows the entire history and future of the world in which you live. Sometimes that robot is Lieutenant Commander Data. These scientificially observed facts are called Scalzi's laws of robotics. A robot can only be one of those four things. Kentucky Route Zero is a game that explores what it might mean for the laws of robotics to be slightly relaxed (not unlike how Star Trek slightly relaxes the intergalactic speed limit), allowing a robot to be multiple types of robot at the same time. That's right, in Kentucky Route Zero, Lieutenant Commander Data puts on a dress, picks up a keytar and plans your destiny from his dive bar. This is a wonderful game that really makes you think about the universe and doesn't contain any disturbing skeletons.

title: Kentucky Route Zero
text: You know that feeling when you take a wrong turn at night, and just keep driving? You never feel anxious or lost, but not quite good either? Kentucky Route Zero manages to capture that feeling. This game has some strong characters. They all have deep, interweaving, backstories. I can't figure out a good way to say this, but I felt like I knew these characters for a long time. I found myself saying “Well yeah, isn't that obvious?” and then realizing that, no, isn’t obvious. I don't know. I can't quite put that feeling into words properly. Just play it and find out. Kentucky Route Zero is cut into 5 episodes, 4 of which have been released. Those episodes are chopped into scenes. The game occasionally would do gimmicky once-scene narrative changes, like having time flow from left to right, or having the scene shot exclusively through security cameras with commentary from security guards. I love that sort of♥♥♥♥♥♥ It keeps you engaged with the story. So about that episodic release schedule. It’s slow, apparently. Very slow. I wouldn't know, I bought this game a while ago. It can take up to a year of an episode. Many people have called it a scam, or accused the devs of abandoning the game. I think that’s bs. Each chapter is longer and higher quality than the last. Each chapter is also riskier than the last. Chapter one was pretty much a side scroller, while chapter three is mostly 3D and has cinematic angles. I would rather have a good game with long development than rushed garbage. But hey, that’s just my opinion. Speaking of cinematics, this game looks pretty damn good. It nails the minimalist low-poly aesthetic. The game’s use of color is pretty great too.  Most of the game is dark and cold, but the bits of psychological horror are warm. It’s a nice change. Overall, this game is amazing. I look forward to re-reviewing this when episode five eventually comes out.

title: Kentucky Route Zero
text: This game is a masterpiece of stunning sound design, subtle minimalist visuals and a compelling narrative that sucks you in. But also? ...have you ever seen Lost?  You know how for every answer, there are 40 more questions?  KR0 feels like that.  It's the most masturbatory hipster magnum opus on Steam; the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child of the gimmicky narrative of House of Leaves(this road goes a certain way BUT ONLY IF YOU POINT IN THAT DIRECTION) wrapped in cringeworthy Vogon bureaucracy fetch quests(you literally have to go back and forth looking up files and talking to clerks), pretentious contemporary art forcing you to interact with it(why am I interacting with this bird cage that sounds like a xylophone), all seasoned with smarmy, hipster, tongue-in-cheek humor, random for random's sake(why are there bears.).  You can just FEEL the beanie-bedecked, Weezer glasses wearing, skinny-jeans-and-curled-beard designers giving each other high fives each time they got a boner when their narrative switched from first person to staticky-vinyl-third-person-observer, or when the shadow hillbillies played bluegrass in the foreground as the characters exited a broken down mine the designers would never see in real life. because they're busy hanging out on the lounge chairs in Starbucks, romanticizing a mountain culture full of 'noble savages' they wish they could appropriate while deep-throating their venti mocha chai unicorn dust latte. Magical realism is my jam - this world they built *is* a compelling and urgent dystopia, and I was begging for a reason to come back to it!  But none of the tidbits are connected.  I don't want backstory about the random hobo on the side of the road, or the janitor at the storage unit place.  I don't need my storylines handed to me on a plate, I enjoy a little reading-between-the-lines and conversatin' about the nature of the narrative... but a couple of hours in all I got was 'hey, this world is kinda weird and that one road works funny.'  And after the hours I put into this, my PC is starting to smell like sandalwood and beard oil, and I kind of hate it.

title: Kentucky Route Zero
text: DISCLAIMER: It's been awhile since I played this game and I am finally getting around to reviewing it. I put off reviewing it for so long because it's such an odd game and I didn't know what to say about it. Anyway, the point is that I am going off of my faulty memory. I liked this game but it's not for everyone. It's really hard to pin down. It plays like the graphical adventure games of olden days--King's Quest, Police Quest, Space Quest, etc. except you don't really collect items in an inventory, neither do you really solve any puzzles. It almost feels like a surreal text adventure populated with quirky characters but with some impressionistic graphics and haunting music to go along with it. It's like a game that Sierra On-Line would have made back in the day, if David Lynch and William Faulkner had worked there. The game feels more like a tone poem. It's eerie at times, but not scary. It can be hauntingly beautiful at times, leaving you feeling melancholy. Sometimes it can be weirdly comical. As I said before, you don't really solve any major puzzles and you only occasionally feel like you are pursuing any sort of goal or are part of any story that is advancing toward any kind of resolution. You sort of go along for the ride and you do have decisions to make, but those are mostly just selecting dialog. The gameplay, what little there is, feels like mostly just adding some subtle nuance to the way the characters interact with each other. Looking back over what I wrote, it can seem like I am being negative about the game, but I can say that it was a very unique experience and I thought that the presentation, however odd, was enjoyable. If you want to try something really different, I suggest you give this game a shot when it goes on sale.

title: KickBeat Steam Edition
text: This is a good addition to the genre of good music driven video games such as Audiosurf 2, Audiosurf 1, and Beat Hazard. It is also quite similar to another great game called One Finger Death Punch. KickBeat combines martial arts fighting and music to create a solid game. The game has a single player campaign Story Mode where you play through all of the songs that come with the game. First as a male character. And then as a female character. As you keep playing and get better scores on the songs that come with the game, you unlock more characters that you can play as. And you also unlock more outfits for the existing characters. You can of course also play this game with your own music files as well. Although in this game, you need to manually set the beats per minute for each custom song that you want to use. Although the game makes it fairly easy for you to do that. The game plays a 15 second section from the start, middle, and end of the song. And all you have to do is just tap the Space bar to the beat of the song. Then you can listen to the final result to make sure that the beats are set properly with the song. Then the song is ready to be played in the game. The game has selectable difficulty levels so you can choose how difficult you want any song to be. It may take some time to get used to playing KickBeat at first because the in game tutorial doesn't really prepare you very well. But keep practicing and you'll learn how to play the game. If you like music driven games like Audiosurf 2, Audiosurf 1, and Beat Hazard, then I recommend KickBeat

Easy to learn, difficult to master should have been the mantra for this games development. title: Killer Instinct
text: Killer Instinct -- an enjoyable fighting game in keeping with Street Fighter and Mortal Kombat. The steam edition is on par with the definitive edition otherwise offered on the Windows store and Xbox. As such, all characters are fully unlocked. Although there are micro transactions, these are entirely optional--as all skins/badges et al. are accessible via regular game play/grinding and are all totally cosmetic. The major two complaints with this iteration of Killer Instinct are as follows: 1. Cross platform play for Ranked Matches is blocked between Steam and Win/Xbox player bases. This seems arbitrary and very short sighted on the part of M$. 2. The online performance test, which is required for online ranked matches, can prohibit players from participating in ranked matches if their system is deemed to be below certain undisclosed thresholds. This "black box" testing is unacceptable as several instances of otherwise viable rigs have been reported as failing this test. However, the feedback afforded from the ingame diagnostic does not give any viable information/suggestions as to what is causing the respective low score (It simply gives a score with a minimum threshold of 1000). This can result in systems, which can run the game perfectly well in unranked matches and single player, being unable to participate in the ranked system. Overall the game is fun and fits well with the original coin-op iterations of KI1 and KI2. However, for online play, due to the opaque performance testing and segregated ranked player bases, cannot be fully recommended. Simply put, the design and implementation of these two elements are abject failures and seem highly arbitrary. Purchase the game for solo play or online unranked play. Do not purchase the game for online ranked play (as you may well be blocked from participating by the game itself). Do not purchase the game if you are keen to complete all achievements -- as several require access to online ranked matches to which you may not have access.

One thing to note is that the main missions are supposed to be like episodes of an anime show.  I'm sure this game would have gotten better reviews if there was an anime show that came first and then this game followed. During the game, like other Suda games, I questioned my life and why I was still playing these games.  It wasn't necessarily boring, but I wanted to hurry up and finish the game and move onto something else.  However, after beating the game, that's where the most fun was had because you can then unlock . Switching between difficulty settings was nicely set up and fluid.  You can press a button and increase or decrease the difficulty whenever on the stage selection screen.  There are also certain parts where you go out on dates with girls and try to sneak peeks at their private areas in order to build up to having sex with them.  There's no nudity, but you might avoid this if your parents/family are around... The combat in this game turned out to be pretty good.  It's not just button mashing to hack away at enemies.  You have to use strategy to beat enemies who are equipped with shields, armor, etc. For those who are achievement hunters, this game will not be a quick one.  It may take me upwards of 50 hours to 100% this game.  However, in the section of guides for this game, someone uploaded his nearly 100% save file.  I haven't tried it (yet?), but you apparently still have to play through the levels and other parts of the game to unlock the achievements for yourself. Should you get this game?  If you like Suda games and/or anime-style hack & slash games, sure!  And, there's definitely $20 worth of effort put into this game to justify the price, combined with some 50 hours of gameplay if you really get into it.  However, you'll probably survive if you skip this game.  I don't recall anything super memorable that would make this a must-buy. text: I gave this a good try, but i just can't like it. The gameplay is mediocre, if you're expecting a Devil May Cry or a God of War - the combat just doesn't deliver. It's a button masher, and I couldn't make it into anything more, no matter how much I tried to use special abilities and attacks, (and I have plenty of experience with action games.) Controls were fine with a controller, (I can't speak for M&B - i didn't try), but it was just boring. As far as art assets and story go... Someone compared this to Lynch.. This is NOT Lynch. Lynch has a soul, and a certain depth... This just felt like someone found an equation for surreal art and simply followed it without actually believing in it. Random stories, obscure humor, characters that have no explanation of why they are there and who are they really, just a ton of disconnected strings all over that don't make up a cohesive whole. I mean, maybe some people are into that, but I'm not, so I can't recommend this. I love Magritte, and Lynch, and in their surreal there is at least something that ties everything together. This game is more like someone just colored a canvas black, added a big red circle, then decided to add a robot arm, and then thought let's throw a unicorn in there for the hell of it, because why not. I guess I'll give this game some points, but only because it's at least something I haven't seen before. And there were some decent comic-book-style cutscene shots that were visually well delivered, I guess. But overall - it was a pretty mediocre ride on most accounts.
